explanations.explanation: Luke says, "And Peter followed at a distance." He's not gone, but he's not up close either. I think he's trying to stay near without standing out. I've tried that at a family cookout when the dishes start piling up.

That would be a bold walk, friend, but it's not what Luke tells us. He says Peter followed "at a distance." Peter is behind the crowd, not beside Jesus. Right at His side is the front row, and Peter is way back in the cheap seats.

Luke says they seized Jesus and led Him away. He says nothing about Peter being tied up. Peter follows on his own and later sits down by a fire in the courtyard. Nobody tied him to anything, friend, he walked in by himself.

She looks at him intently in the firelight and says, "This man also was with Him." She's talking about Jesus, the One who was just taken. Nobody else in the courtyard has said a word yet. She goes first, and she doesn't whisper.

explanations.answer: He works for the high priest
explanations.explanation: Luke doesn't say anything like that. She says Peter "also was with Him," and the "Him" is Jesus. Peter is a follower of Jesus here, not a worker in the high priest's house. That job title never comes up in this passage.
That's not what she says, baker. A stranger wouldn't get a long look in the firelight. She says, "This man also was with Him." She thinks she knows exactly who he is.
It's the other way around, friend. Peter says, "Woman, I do not know Him." She says he was with Jesus, and he says he doesn't know Him. That's a denial, not an admission.
Right. When the servant girl says he was with Jesus, Peter answers, "Woman, I do not know Him." He doesn't say he knows Jesus. He says he doesn't know Him at all.
Luke says someone else saw Peter and said, "You also are one of them." Peter answered, "Man, I am not." That's two for two. He's not even leaving the door cracked.
Peter doesn't change his answer. When someone says, "You also are one of them," he replies, "Man, I am not." Same story as before, from a different mouth. It's still a denial.

The man insists, "Certainly this man was with Him, for he too is a Galilean." Galilee is the region Jesus is from, and the man says Peter is from there too. That's his whole case. He says it like he's got proof.
Luke doesn't mention any staring from Peter. The man gives one reason, and it's about where Peter is from: "for he too is a Galilean." It's not about where Peter is looking.

explanations.answer: Peter came in with the crowd
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text, friend. The man says Peter "too is a Galilean." He's pointing at Peter's home region, not at how he got into the courtyard. Nobody says a word about the crowd.

Luke says, "And immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed." Peter doesn't even get to finish his sentence. That timing is something, friend. That rooster showed up like it had a meeting on the calendar.
Luke says nothing about the fire going out. The fire in the courtyard is just where Peter sits. What happens while he's still speaking is that "the rooster crowed."
No guard grabs anybody in these verses. Peter is talking, and "immediately, while he was still speaking, the rooster crowed." The sound is what interrupts him, not a hand.
Luke says, "And the Lord turned and looked at Peter." Jesus is the Lord here. The text gives us the look, and then Peter remembers. Sometimes one look says it all, baker.
It's true, friend. After the rooster crows, "the Lord turned and looked at Peter." The Lord is Jesus. Right after that look, Peter remembers what he'd been told.

The Lord told Peter, "Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times." Count them in the courtyard: the servant girl, then someone else, then another man. That's three. Peter hears it all play out in his head.
Close, but the Lord said three. He told Peter, "Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times." Peter gets all three in this very courtyard, one answer at a time.

Seven is a big number, friend, but it's not the one. The Lord said, "Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times." That's the number Peter remembers, and it matches the three people who spoke to him.

Luke says, "And he went outside and wept bitterly." He remembers the Lord's words, and then he goes out and weeps. I think this is one of the saddest moments in the whole story. No joke from me here, friend.
Luke doesn't say Peter complains. He says Peter "went outside and wept bitterly." That's grief, not grumbling. I think he's hurting, friend.
No shouting here. Luke says he "went outside and wept bitterly." He steps away from the courtyard, and the tears come. I think this one is quiet and heavy.

explanations.answer: That He prophesy who hit Him
explanations.explanation: The men blindfold Him and keep demanding, "Prophesy! Who hit You?" They're mocking Him while they hit Him. It's a hard scene, friend. I'll let Luke's words stand.

explanations.answer: That He bow to the high priest
explanations.explanation: Luke doesn't say that. The demand he records is "Prophesy! Who hit You?" It comes while Jesus is blindfolded. It's a hard moment, and the text is plain about it.

explanations.answer: That He call His disciples back
explanations.explanation: That isn't in these verses. What the men keep demanding is, "Prophesy! Who hit You?" They're mocking Him while they're holding Him. It's heavy, friend.
Luke says, "At daybreak the council of the elders of the people, both the chief priests and scribes, met together." The night is over, and the council gathers. Daybreak is when they sit down.
Luke puts it at daybreak. He says, "At daybreak the council of the elders of the people… met together." The sun is coming up when they gather. It's not the middle of the night.
Luke says the council of the elders of the people is made up of "both the chief priests and scribes." They meet together at daybreak. Then they lead Jesus into their Sanhedrin, their council hall.

Not here, friend. Pilate, governor of Judea, and Herod, ruler of Galilee (Luke 3:1), aren't named in this meeting. Luke says this council is "both the chief priests and scribes." Pilate and Herod come into the story later (Luke 23:1, 7).
Luke doesn't list any soldiers on this council. He says it's "the council of the elders of the people, both the chief priests and scribes." Those are the ones who gather and lead Jesus in.
It's the opposite, friend. Jesus says, "If I tell you, you will not believe." He's saying they won't believe, not that they will. That's what the text says.
Right. When the council says, "If You are the Christ, tell us," Jesus answers, "If I tell you, you will not believe." He says they will not believe. He doesn't say they will.
Jesus says, "And if I ask you a question, you will not answer." So whether He tells them or asks them, He says it won't go anywhere. It's a quiet line, friend, and Luke leaves it as it is.
Luke doesn't say that. Jesus says, "And if I ask you a question, you will not answer." It's about silence, not laughter. Nothing is said about laughing.
No crowd comes into this part. Jesus says, "And if I ask you a question, you will not answer." The answer isn't handed off to anyone. It just doesn't come.

explanations.answer: If He is the Son of God
explanations.explanation: After Jesus speaks of the Son of Man, the whole council asks, "Are You then the Son of God?" They all ask it together. Jesus replies, "You say that I am."

explanations.answer: If He is the king of Israel
explanations.explanation: That's not the question in these verses. They all ask, "Are You then the Son of God?" It's a question about who He is, and it comes right after He mentions the Son of Man.

explanations.answer: If He is a prophet from Galilee
explanations.explanation: Not this time, baker. The whole council asks, "Are You then the Son of God?" Galilee doesn't come up in their question. Jesus answers, "You say that I am."
They say the opposite, friend. They declare, "Why do we need any more testimony?" They're saying they don't need more. They heard it for themselves.
Right. The council says, "Why do we need any more testimony? We have heard it for ourselves from His own lips." They say they're done needing testimony. They believe they've heard enough.
